title: Counterfactual Istidlal — Curated Questions Across Book 02
description: A concise, carefully curated bank for the Introduction and every chapter. Answers include direct links to relevant Qur'anic verses and source passages. Hypothetical conclusions are inferences, not claims that classical sources explicitly answered these exact questions.

coverage.selection_policy: Curated for distinct learning value; no quota per concept.

counterfactuals.prompt: Suppose 'Ali had used deception to gain political power, sincerely intending to govern justly afterward. If the outcome were better, what would still be at stake?
counterfactuals.answer: The immediate result would not settle the moral or institutional cost. In Nahj al-Balagha 200, 'Ali distinguishes political cunning from deception that crosses moral limits; Qur'an 4:135 commands justice even when it cuts against our own interests. If a ruler normalizes deception whenever he claims a good end, successors can use the same excuse for self-interest. This concerns deceptive acquisition of authority; any specific exception, such as a narrowly defined wartime tactic, needs its own evidence rather than being generalized.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: A claimed good end does not automatically legitimize a method that teaches future rulers to deceive.

counterfactuals.prompt: Suppose paying powerful supporters special stipends really would have prevented a civil war. Would that prove 'Ali should have sacrificed the rights of poorer people?
counterfactuals.answer: It might show that refusing favoritism carried a real political cost, but not that the injustice became right. Qur'an 4:135 requires standing for justice even against one's own interests, and 5:8 warns that even hostility must not pull a person away from justice. Letter 53 of Nahj al-Balagha likewise frames governance around care for the vulnerable. The counterfactual forces us to ask not only what outcome was likely, but whose rights were treated as expendable to achieve it.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: Political effectiveness matters, but it cannot by itself cancel the rights of people with less power.

counterfactuals.prompt: Suppose the commanders raising Qur'ans on spears sincerely wanted to stop bloodshed. Why might the tactic still be religiously misleading?
counterfactuals.answer: A sincere motive does not guarantee that the conclusion drawn from a symbol is sound. In Sermon 125, 'Ali explains that people must speak and interpret through the Qur'an; the physical presence of its pages cannot decide a political dispute by itself. Qur'an 6:57 affirms God's judgment, but quoting it does not remove the need to understand what it means in context. The danger is that a sacred sign can pressure people to stop reasoning precisely when careful judgment is most needed.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: Reverence for scripture requires understanding and applying it, not treating its appearance as a substitute for reasoning.

counterfactuals.prompt: Suppose the arbitrators had ruled in 'Ali's favor. Would that vindicate the Kharijite claim that appointing human arbitrators is itself blasphemy?
counterfactuals.answer: No: a favorable result would not repair a faulty principle, just as an unfavorable result cannot prove every form of arbitration illegitimate. Sermon 125 argues that the Qur'an needs people to interpret and apply it; Qur'an 4:59 directs believers to refer disputes to Allah and the Messenger, which itself requires human deliberation about what that reference entails. The proper test is whether judgment remains accountable to revelation, not whether human judgment disappears.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: Judge a principle by its reasoning and limits, not merely by whether one decision succeeds.

counterfactuals.prompt: Suppose a community were intensely devout but had never learned how to interpret the Qur'an carefully. Would visible piety make its judgments more trustworthy?
counterfactuals.answer: Not by itself. Mutahhari presents the Kharijites as dangerous precisely because striking outward devotion coexisted with shallow understanding. Qur'an 17:36 warns against following what one does not know, while 'Ali's words in Sermon 122 distinguish the Qur'an's recitation from understanding its meaning. Devotion can motivate learning, but when it is treated as proof that one's interpretation cannot be wrong, it can shield error from correction.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: Sincerity and visible worship are not substitutes for knowledge, humility, and sound interpretation.

counterfactuals.prompt: Suppose the Kharijites continued insulting 'Ali but never turned to armed violence. Should he silence them to protect the dignity of government?
counterfactuals.answer: Not automatically. Mutahhari emphasizes that 'Ali tolerated their dissent and did not cut their treasury share simply because they opposed him. Qur'an 49:9 distinguishes conflict that calls for reconciliation from the duty to restrain an aggressor; it does not make every hostile disagreement equivalent to armed rebellion. The distinction matters because a ruler who treats criticism as violence can turn public authority into a shield against correction.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: A government should distinguish offensive speech and dissent from a real, evidence-based threat of violence.

counterfactuals.prompt: Suppose a person commits a serious sin but remains Muslim and seeks repentance. Does the sin alone justify declaring that person outside Islam?
counterfactuals.answer: No. Condemning an act and declaring a person outside the faith are different judgments with different evidentiary burdens. Qur'an 49:9 still describes two fighting parties as believers while commanding reconciliation, and 4:94 warns believers not to casually deny another's faith. Mutahhari's account of Kharijite doctrine shows how collapsing every serious sin into total exclusion can turn moral criticism into sectarian violence.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: Moral accountability does not license careless judgments about another person's entire religious identity.

counterfactuals.prompt: Suppose 'Ali defeated the Kharijites at Nahrawan and then ordered the killing of every remaining sympathizer, including those who had laid down their arms. Would that be justified as prevention?
counterfactuals.answer: No: a past affiliation or mistaken doctrine cannot by itself establish present guilt or an active threat. Mutahhari reports 'Ali's final instruction not to keep killing Kharijites after him, distinguishing people who seek truth but err from those who pursue falsehood deliberately. Qur'an 5:8 commands justice even toward those one dislikes. Preventing future harm requires evidence and proportionate judgment, not collective revenge.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: Justice after conflict means distinguishing present conduct and credible danger from labels and revenge.

counterfactuals.prompt: Suppose a rumor about a revered scholar were repeated by ten respected teachers. Could a student safely repeat it without checking the original evidence?
counterfactuals.answer: No. Repetition and reputation do not turn a report into verified knowledge. Qur'an 49:6 instructs believers to verify reports before acting on them, and 17:36 warns against following what one does not know. Mutahhari's Iqbal/Ja'far-Sadiq example shows how a careless reading can become a false accusation as it passes from person to person. The responsible response is to inspect the original context before forwarding the claim.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: The credibility of a chain of repeaters cannot replace checking the original evidence and context.

counterfactuals.prompt: Suppose Ibn Muljam sincerely believed that killing 'Ali was an act of worship. Would sincerity make his act morally sound?
counterfactuals.answer: No. Sincerity describes a person's subjective conviction; it does not prove that the conviction is true or that the action is just. Qur'an 17:36 warns against acting without knowledge, and the chapter's account of the Kharijites shows how religious certainty can be used to excuse grave wrongdoing. This does not mean motives are irrelevant; it means intention must be assessed alongside knowledge, evidence, and the moral nature of the act.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: A sincere intention cannot turn an unjust act into a justified one when the underlying judgment is false.

counterfactuals.prompt: If every Imam had followed the same visible political strategy in every era, would that necessarily have produced greater fidelity to Islam?
counterfactuals.answer: Not necessarily. Mutahhari's argument is that the Imams faced different threats and opportunities while preserving the same core commitments. [Qur'an 22:39](https://quran.com/22/39) connects permission to fight with being wronged; it does not prescribe identical action in every circumstance. The contrast between al-Husayn's revolt and other Imams' restraint asks us to judge strategy against its conditions and purpose, not turn one historical response into a universal script.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: A stable moral purpose can require different outward strategies when circumstances and duties differ.

counterfactuals.prompt: If an Imam narrated a Prophetic practice but did not personally follow it in a later era, should we assume he contradicted the Prophet?
counterfactuals.answer: Not before asking whether the practice was a permanent command or a response to a particular circumstance. Mutahhari uses the beard-dyeing example to distinguish outward form from underlying purpose. [Qur'an 16:90](https://quran.com/16/90) gives enduring moral principles, while a specific historical tactic may have a narrower purpose. This supports careful interpretation, not dismissing inconvenient reports: context and evidence must establish whether a ruling is general or situational.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: Before calling a contradiction, distinguish the lasting principle from a context-specific application.

counterfactuals.prompt: If peace and armed resistance were judged by which one looks braver, what important part of the al-Hassan question would be missed?
counterfactuals.answer: It would replace moral and jurisprudential analysis with a performance test. Mutahhari rejects explaining al-Hassan and al-Husayn as merely having different temperaments. [Qur'an 49:9](https://quran.com/49/9) begins with reconciliation between fighting believers and then addresses persistent aggression; [Qur'an 22:39](https://quran.com/22/39) situates fighting in a context of being wronged. Neither passage makes one response obligatory in every situation. We must examine what each choice could accomplish and what principles it preserved.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: Courage is not identical to fighting; ask which response fits the duty and circumstances.

counterfactuals.prompt: Suppose a truce stopped immediate bloodshed but gave the other side an unlimited opportunity to attack later. Would the word 'peace' alone make it sound?
counterfactuals.answer: No. The chapter treats peace as a means governed by terms, duration, and likely consequences—not as a self-validating label. [Qur'an 8:61](https://quran.com/8/61) directs believers to incline toward peace when the opposing side genuinely inclines toward it; it does not require ignoring evidence of bad faith or abandoning safeguards. One must ask whether the agreement serves a legitimate protective purpose and whether its terms are clear enough to evaluate.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: A peace agreement must be judged by its terms and purpose, not its name alone.

counterfactuals.prompt: If al-Hassan's peace and al-Husayn's revolt were judged only by immediate outcomes, why would that be an unreliable moral test?
counterfactuals.answer: Immediate outcomes alone cannot tell us whether a decision was justified by the conditions known at the time. Mutahhari distinguishes their political positions, military balance, public demands, and the role each action played in exposing injustice. The Qur'an recognizes reconciliation ([49:9](https://quran.com/49/9)) and a context for resisting oppression ([22:39](https://quran.com/22/39)); neither verse makes one response obligatory in every situation. Historical uncertainty does not disappear in hindsight.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: Judge a decision by its duties, context, and foreseeable consequences—not hindsight alone.

counterfactuals.prompt: Suppose al-Hassan's treaty had preserved his life but required him to endorse every act of Mu'awiyah's government. Would survival alone justify accepting it?
counterfactuals.answer: Survival is a serious consideration, but a term requiring the Imam to validate injustice would change the moral meaning of the agreement. [Qur'an 4:135](https://quran.com/4/135) commands standing firmly for justice even when personally costly; it is therefore not enough to ask whether a treaty prevents immediate death. One must also ask what public truth it forces a person to affirm or conceal.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: Preserving life and accepting a ruler's legitimacy are separate questions; treaty terms matter.

counterfactuals.prompt: If Imam Zayn al-'Abidin's spirituality were measured only by private worship, what part of Mutahhari's portrait would disappear?
counterfactuals.answer: His spirituality would be separated from its social consequences. Mutahhari emphasizes that the Imam welcomed people who were poor, isolated, or stigmatized and served fellow pilgrims without relying on his status. [Qur'an 107:1–7](https://quran.com/107/1-7) criticizes religious performance that neglects the needy, while [Qur'an 4:36](https://quran.com/4/36) commands kindness to vulnerable neighbors and travelers. The point is not to diminish worship, but to ask whether worship is forming compassion and responsibility.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: Spirituality is incomplete when devotion does not deepen care for people who are easily overlooked.

counterfactuals.prompt: Suppose pilgrims had known the Imam's identity from the beginning and treated him as an honored leader. What might anonymous service teach that praise could not?
counterfactuals.answer: Anonymous service makes the act itself, rather than status or social return, the center of attention. It also tests whether a person will perform humble work without the prestige of serving a famous figure. [Qur'an 2:271](https://quran.com/2/271) notes the value of giving charity privately as well as openly; it does not make secrecy mandatory, but helps explain why hidden service can protect sincerity from becoming a performance.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: Hidden service can test sincerity by removing the social reward that accompanies a revered name.

counterfactuals.prompt: If a political organizer used the language of the Ahl al-Bayt but secretly offered power to rival claimants, what would that reveal about the offer?
counterfactuals.answer: It would weaken the claim that the organizer was acting from settled commitment to one rightful leader. Mutahhari presents Abu Salmah's parallel letters as evidence that a sacred slogan and sincere allegiance are not the same thing. [Qur'an 61:2–3](https://quran.com/61/2-3) rebukes the gap between professed words and conduct; it is a general principle, not a direct verdict on Abu Salmah. The practical test is whether actions and commitments match the public claim.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: A movement's slogans are not proof of its loyalty; test its conduct and commitments.

counterfactuals.prompt: Suppose Muhammad Nafs al-Zakiyyah's uprising opposed oppression, but his identification as the Promised Mahdi remained unproven. Could one support the cause while rejecting that claim?
counterfactuals.answer: Yes; those are distinct judgments. The chapter reports Imam al-Sadiq distinguishing the principle of resisting oppression from accepting a specific claimant as the Promised Mahdi. [Qur'an 17:36](https://quran.com/17/36) warns against following what one has no knowledge of, so a worthy cause cannot substitute for evidence about a person's identity or status. This does not settle every question about supporting the uprising; it prevents one unproven claim from being smuggled in with another moral claim.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: Support for a just aim does not establish every claim made by the movement pursuing it.

counterfactuals.prompt: If Imam Musa al-Kazim could have left prison by making a false confession that legitimized Harun's accusation, would release alone make that choice wise?
counterfactuals.answer: Release would matter, but the confession would also change the public meaning of the imprisonment: it could make coercion appear justified. Mutahhari presents the Imam's refusal as a refusal to validate a charge he did not accept. [Qur'an 33:70](https://quran.com/33/70) commands believers to speak rightly; it is a general principle, not a direct ruling on this historical report. The hypothetical asks us to weigh survival against whether a compelled statement would mislead others or surrender the truth.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: A benefit gained by a false public confession may carry a cost beyond the person making it.

counterfactuals.prompt: If every form of work connected to an unjust ruler were forbidden, how could a believer ever protect people from harm within a corrupt administration?
counterfactuals.answer: A blanket rule would erase the distinction the chapter draws between cooperation that serves the ruler's interests and work that genuinely protects people. Prophet Yusuf asks to manage the storehouses because he is capable ([Qur'an 12:55](https://quran.com/12/55)); that example does not make every appointment under an unjust ruler permissible. Purpose, likely effects, alternatives, and whether the role helps or legitimizes wrongdoing still require scrutiny.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: Cooperation must be judged by what it enables and whom it serves, not by the job title alone.

counterfactuals.prompt: If Ma'mun's motives for appointing Imam al-Rida were uncertain, what would go wrong if a teacher presented one theory as established fact?
counterfactuals.answer: The teacher would erase the distinction Mutahhari makes between reported events and competing explanations of motive. The summons, refusal, threat, and condition of non-interference are treated differently from hypotheses about Ma'mun's sincerity or political calculation. [Qur'an 17:36](https://quran.com/17/36) warns against following what one does not know; here that means labeling uncertainty honestly, not refusing to interpret evidence. A plausible explanation should remain a hypothesis until the sources justify stronger confidence.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: Historical reasoning must label inference as inference, especially when claiming to know another person's motives.

counterfactuals.prompt: Suppose Imam al-Rida accepted the succession only after an explicit threat to his life. Would acceptance by itself prove that he endorsed Ma'mun's legitimacy?
counterfactuals.answer: No. Consent under coercion and voluntary endorsement are not equivalent, and the chapter reports that the Imam accepted only after refusing and setting a condition of non-interference. Prophet Yusuf's request for a public office ([Qur'an 12:55](https://quran.com/12/55)) is a separate case of seeking a beneficial role; it cannot erase the difference between voluntary service and compelled acceptance. The terms and surrounding evidence determine what the action signifies.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: An outward title does not by itself reveal whether the person accepted its political meaning freely.

counterfactuals.prompt: If working inside an unjust government can sometimes protect the public, what evidence distinguishes principled service from becoming a tool of oppression?
counterfactuals.answer: The mere fact that an office offers influence is not enough. Mutahhari contrasts Safwan Jammal's financially motivated service with 'Ali ibn Yaqtin's position, which could protect believers, and discusses Yusuf's public role as an analogy. [Qur'an 12:55](https://quran.com/12/55) supports Yusuf's request in its specific context; it is not a universal license to serve tyrants. Ask whether the role reduces injustice, whether wrongful orders can be refused, and whether the public benefit is real rather than cover for private gain.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: Service under a ruler is defensible only when its purpose and actual effects can be morally defended.

counterfactuals.prompt: Suppose the crown-prince title brought Imam al-Rida prestige but no power to change government decisions. Why would the condition of non-interference still matter?
counterfactuals.answer: It marks a boundary between holding a public title and accepting responsibility for the ruler's actions. The chapter treats the condition, the Imam's earlier refusal, and his independent conduct as evidence that the title should not be read as simple endorsement. [Qur'an 4:135](https://quran.com/4/135) calls for justice even when it is personally costly; a ceremonial role cannot be judged solely by prestige if it might make an unjust arrangement appear legitimate.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: A public title and practical responsibility differ; examine the terms and the message the role sends.

counterfactuals.prompt: If a ruler believed a future reformer would threaten his dynasty, could surveillance and force prove that the ruler's fear was justified?
counterfactuals.answer: They could reveal the ruler's fear, but not prove that the feared claim was false or that repression was just. Mutahhari compares the authorities' efforts with Pharaoh's oppression in the Qur'anic account ([28:4–6](https://quran.com/28/4-6)); this is an analogy about power trying to control a perceived threat, not independent proof of every historical detail. Explaining why a ruler acts is different from establishing whether the action is right.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: A ruler's attempt to suppress a belief reveals policy or fear, not proof that the belief is false.

counterfactuals.prompt: If the community could not openly consult the Imam under surveillance, would religious guidance and responsibility simply disappear?
counterfactuals.answer: Not necessarily. The chapter describes Jaddah and Hakimah Khatun as helping preserve guidance and answer practical questions under extraordinary constraints. [Qur'an 16:43](https://quran.com/16/43) instructs people to ask those who possess knowledge when they do not know; applying that general principle still requires care about qualification and what a report establishes. Restricted access can change how a community seeks guidance without making verification optional.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: Restricted access can change how a community seeks guidance without making careful knowledge-seeking optional.

counterfactuals.prompt: Suppose a powerful person could violate others' rights without risking retaliation. If justice depended only on self-interest, what reason would remain for restraint?
counterfactuals.answer: The theory would struggle precisely where its incentive disappears. Mutahhari's critique asks whether justice remains binding when someone becomes powerful enough to avoid consequences. [Qur'an 4:135](https://quran.com/4/135) commands justice even against one's own interests, and [Letter 53 of Nahj al-Balagha](https://al-islam.org/nahjul-balagha-part-2-letters-and-sayings/letter-53-order-malik-al-ashtar) emphasizes a ruler's duty toward people with less power. These sources do not replace the philosophical argument; they show the ethical standard the chapter asks us to explain.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: A theory of justice must explain why the powerful should act justly when injustice would benefit them.

counterfactuals.prompt: If justice means giving everyone exactly the same thing in every circumstance, could identical treatment itself become unfair?
counterfactuals.answer: Yes. Equal dignity does not always imply identical allocation where needs, responsibilities, or relevant qualifications differ. Mutahhari distinguishes justice from mechanical sameness; [Qur'an 5:8](https://quran.com/5/8) requires justice even when emotions pull us away from it, while [Letter 53 of Nahj al-Balagha](https://al-islam.org/nahjul-balagha-part-2-letters-and-sayings/letter-53-order-malik-al-ashtar) directs a governor's attention to the vulnerable. The difficult task is to show that different treatment rests on a relevant reason rather than favoritism or prejudice.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: Fairness requires relevant reasons for different treatment, not automatic sameness or arbitrary preference.

counterfactuals.prompt: If many people across history claimed to be the Promised Mahdi, would that alone disprove the belief—or prove any one claimant genuine?
counterfactuals.answer: Neither conclusion follows. A history of false or disputed claimants can show that the idea had real influence, but it cannot by itself establish or refute the identity of the promised figure. Mutahhari distinguishes historical claims from evidence offered for them. [Qur'an 17:36](https://quran.com/17/36) warns against following what one has no knowledge of, while [Qur'an 21:105](https://quran.com/21/105) is discussed as a general foundation concerning the righteous inheriting the earth—not as a standalone identification of a particular claimant.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: Evidence for a general promise and evidence that a particular person fulfills it are different questions.

counterfactuals.prompt: Suppose someone argued that society must become more corrupt before the Imam can reappear, so believers should stop reforming it. What is the flaw in that reasoning?
counterfactuals.answer: It turns a description of future events into permission to help produce the corruption believers should resist. Mutahhari rejects the claim that awaiting reappearance means abandoning reform or religious duties. [Qur'an 7:56](https://quran.com/7/56) warns against spreading corruption on earth after it has been set right, and [Qur'an 11:88](https://quran.com/11/88) presents reform as a positive aim. These verses do not predict the timing of reappearance; they challenge the inference that one should deliberately worsen society to hasten it.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: Awaiting a promised just future is not permission to abandon present duties or manufacture injustice.

counterfactuals.prompt: If belief in the Mahdi's future victory guaranteed that justice would eventually prevail, why would prayer, reform, and social responsibility still matter now?
counterfactuals.answer: Because the promised outcome does not logically cancel present obligations. Mutahhari treats genuine awaiting as active responsibility, not passive expectation or deliberate corruption. [Qur'an 11:88](https://quran.com/11/88) describes the aim of reform, and [Qur'an 5:8](https://quran.com/5/8) requires justice even when difficult. Belief in future transformation should intensify commitment to the values it promises, rather than become an excuse to postpone them.
counterfactuals.istidlal_takeaway: Hope in future justice should motivate present justice, not replace it.
